overview: Arm Holdings designs and licenses the CPU, GPU, NPU and system IP that underpins the vast majority of the world's smartphones, and is expanding rapidly into data center/AI compute, automotive and IoT. Arm's business model is licensing-plus-royalty: customers (semiconductor companies, OEMs and cloud service providers) pay an upfront or annual license fee for IP access and then a per-chip royalty on every unit shipped, creating a long-tail, high-margin royalty annuity on top of lumpier license revenue. In March 2026 Arm took its first step beyond pure IP licensing by launching the Arm AGI CPU, a production silicon product for AI data centers co-developed with Meta, moving the company into direct competition with some of its own semiconductor customers. Arm is majority owned (~86.4%) and controlled by SoftBank Group, trades as Nasdaq ADSs (1 ADS = 1 ordinary share), and reports on a UK/US dual-listed basis with a March 31 fiscal year end.

business_model.summary: Two-part model: (1) License and other revenue - upfront/annual fees for access to CPU/GPU/NPU/system IP and Compute Subsystems (CSS), recognized partly at a point in time and partly ratably (subscription-style 'Total Access'/'Flexible Access' deals); (2) Royalty revenue - a per-unit fee (percent of ASP or fixed fee per chip) collected on substantially every chip shipped using Arm IP, recognized when the customer ships. FY2026: License & Other revenue $2,307M (47% of total, +25% YoY) vs Royalty revenue $2,613M (53% of total, +21% YoY) on total revenue of $4,920M (+23% YoY). Licensing bookings are a leading indicator of future royalties (royalty revenue lags a new license by 2-5 years as chips tape out and ramp). The FY2026 divestiture of the Artisan foundation-IP business (sold to Cadence for a $131M pre-tax gain) narrowed the portfolio to core CPU/GPU/NPU/system IP and CSS, while the pending ~$265M acquisition of DreamBig Semiconductor adds advanced networking/chiplet capability. Beginning March 2026, Arm added a third, structurally different revenue stream: production silicon (Arm AGI CPU), which carries materially different margins, inventory/working-capital needs and sales cycles than the asset-light IP business; management has guided to up to $2B of cumulative AGI CPU revenue across FY2027-28 and talked publicly of a multi-year path toward ~$15B of annual silicon revenue.

revenue_streams.name: Royalty revenue (per-chip, all end markets)
revenue_streams.trend: growing - mobile mature, data center/AI the fastest-growing driver

revenue_streams.name: License and other revenue (upfront/subscription IP fees, CSS)
revenue_streams.trend: growing - strong FY2026/Q2 FY2027 bookings seen as leading indicator

revenue_streams.name: Production silicon (Arm AGI CPU) - new FY2027
revenue_streams.trend: emerging - first commercial deliveries targeted Q4 FY2027

business_model.customer_type: B2B - semiconductor companies, OEMs, and cloud service providers/hyperscalers (Apple, Qualcomm, MediaTek, Samsung, NVIDIA, AWS, Google, Microsoft, Meta and others); access to the PRC market is almost entirely intermediated through the separately controlled Arm China joint venture
business_model.geographic_mix: FY2026 revenue by customer HQ: United States 36% ($1,761M), PRC 18% ($874M, includes Arm China relationship), Japan 17% ($825M), Taiwan 14% ($695M), South Korea 8% ($392M), Other 8% ($373M). Revenue attributable to the Arm China relationship specifically was ~16% of total revenue in FY2026 (down from 21% in FY2024 as other geographies, especially data center, have grown faster).

main_competitors: RISC-V open-standard architecture (and the RISC-V International ecosystem backed by some of Arm's own customers)
In-house/proprietary silicon at hyperscalers and OEMs (Apple, Google, AWS Graviton, Microsoft, Qualcomm/Nuvia)
Arm China (independently operated JV, can develop certain non-core-architecture derivative IP)
Emerging AI-accelerator vendors reducing the relative importance of the CPU in some workloads
competitive_position.market_position: Arm holds an estimated >99% share of the mobile applications-processor market (royalty revenue from mobile = ~43% of FY2026 royalty revenue) and is the dominant architecture in IoT/embedded and a large share of automotive IVI/ADAS. Its newest and fastest-growing beachhead is cloud/data center: Arm-based share of silicon deployed by top hyperscalers reportedly rose from ~15% in calendar 2024 to >50% in calendar 2025, with management targeting >60% by end of calendar 2026 (data center royalties doubled YoY in the most recent quarter). Arm is a clear #1 in licensable CPU IP but a much smaller player in absolute dollar terms than x86 incumbents and the hyperscalers it is trying to displace.

moat_factors.description: 22+ million developers, virtually every major OS, compiler, and toolchain targets Arm first or natively; 350+ billion cumulative Arm-based chips shipped create a self-reinforcing software/tooling moat that is very hard for a new architecture to replicate quickly.

Customers invest 2-3 years to design a new Arm-based processor and another 2-3 years to bring a chip to market; once software and tooling are built around an architecture, customers rarely switch until the next generational redesign.

~8,600 issued patents plus ~2,750 pending; tiered licensing (Total Access, Flexible Access, CSS, TLA, Architecture License) locks in multi-year recurring relationships and lets Arm monetize a single R&D investment across many customers.

Arm amortizes design/verification costs across dozens of licensees, letting it undercut the cost of in-house core design for most customers - though the largest hyperscalers increasingly have the scale to design in-house.
No meaningful regulatory moat; if anything, SoftBank's 86.4% control and the independently operated Arm China structure are governance complications rather than advantages for minority holders.

weaknesses: Customer concentration: top five customers (including Arm China and SoftBank Group) collectively represented ~57% of FY2026 revenue, with Arm China alone ~16%

RISC-V is free and open-source, and several of Arm's own large customers (and a dedicated RISC-V automotive joint venture announced by a group of customers/competitors in 2023) are actively investing in it as a hedge/alternative, especially for cost-sensitive or sovereign-technology use cases

Structural conflict of interest: Arm's expansion into its own production silicon (Arm AGI CPU) competes directly with some licensing customers, risking disintermediation, pricing pushback, or loss of goodwill from the semiconductor companies and OEMs Arm still depends on for the bulk of its revenue

No operational control over Arm China (its primary access point to the PRC, ~16-18% of revenue), which has its own board, has a history of governance disputes (Allen Wu litigation) and payment/data-access friction

SoftBank controls ~86.4% of shares and exercises board influence (CEO Rene Haas also now holds a part-time SoftBank Group International CEO role), creating related-party and conflict-of-interest risk for minority ADS holders
Active, unresolved litigation with Qualcomm/Nuvia over architecture license terms, with a new trial expected Q4 calendar 2026

growth_drivers: AI/data center buildout: Neoverse-based server CPUs gaining rapid hyperscaler share (>50% in CY2025, targeting >60% by end CY2026); data center royalties doubled YoY in the latest quarter and management frames Cloud AI as the fastest-growing of Arm's three AI domains

Entry into production silicon with the Arm AGI CPU (first delivered Q4 FY2027, Meta as lead co-development partner, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure as a disclosed early adopter) - a structurally new, higher-dollar-content revenue stream management has guided to up to $2B cumulative revenue in FY2027-28 and described publicly as a path to a multi-billion-dollar silicon business over several years
Compute Subsystems (CSS) and 'Total Access'/'Flexible Access' subscription licensing models, which bundle more pre-integrated IP per deal and lift average revenue per customer/design
Armv9-based royalty uplift: newer architecture generations and added AI acceleration instructions carry higher per-chip royalty rates than legacy Armv8 designs as the installed base transitions
Automotive and robotics (Physical AI) as ADAS, electrification and software-defined vehicle architectures require materially more compute per vehicle than legacy designs
Continued double-digit license bookings growth (FY2026 License & Other revenue +25% YoY, Q2 FY2027 +50% YoY) viewed by management as a leading indicator of royalty growth 2-5 years out

Selective M&A to fill technology gaps (pending ~$265M DreamBig Semiconductor networking/chiplet acquisition) while divesting non-core assets (Artisan foundation IP sold to Cadence for $131M gain in FY2026)

Management's long-term TAM narrative: company materials cite a serviceable AI-related addressable market expanding from roughly $400-500B in FY2026 to well over $1 trillion-plus by FY2031, with data center CPU capacity needs framed as a >$100B opportunity by 2030 as agentic AI scales

business.description: Top five customers ~57% of FY2026 revenue; Arm China alone ~16%. Loss, renegotiation, or vertical integration by any major customer (Apple, Qualcomm, NVIDIA, MediaTek, a hyperscaler) would be highly dilutive to revenue.

Free, open-source RISC-V is being adopted by some of Arm's own licensees (including a dedicated automotive-focused RISC-V joint venture announced by a group of Arm customers/competitors) as a lower-cost or sovereign-technology alternative, particularly in China, automotive, and cost-sensitive embedded markets.

The Arm AGI CPU and other integrated compute products create real/perceived competitive conflicts with semiconductor and systems customers who have historically licensed Arm IP; management explicitly flags risk of customers reducing business, withholding roadmap information, or pursuing legal action in response.

Large customers increasingly design their own cores under architecture license rather than using off-the-shelf Arm processor IP (e.g., the Qualcomm/Nuvia dispute), and several of Arm's biggest customers are also developing bespoke AI accelerators that could shrink the relative importance of the general-purpose CPU over time.

Ongoing multi-front litigation over Nuvia's Architecture License Agreement and Qualcomm's own ALA; a split jury verdict already went partly against Arm (appeal pending) and a further trial on Qualcomm's separate claims is expected Q4 calendar 2026.

Foundry/supply chain dependence, inventory, yield, and working-capital risk are new to Arm's historically asset-light model as it ramps Arm AGI CPU manufacturing through third-party foundries (e.g., TSMC).
License revenue timing depends on a limited number of high-value deals signed per quarter; results can swing significantly between periods.

financial.description: Arm China has a history of payment delays and data-access friction; receivables and credit-loss allowances tied to Arm China (~$17-28M allowance) are a recurring item, and PRC capital-control rules can delay repatriation of PRC-sourced cash.

Share-based compensation is large and growing (pre-tax SBC cost ~$720M in H1 FY2027 vs ~$506M in H1 FY2026, +42% YoY), a meaningful drag on GAAP profitability and a source of dilution via RSU/PSU vesting.
Reports in USD but has UK cost base and revenue from Japan, Taiwan, Korea and other non-USD regions, creating translation and transaction FX exposure.

regulatory.risk: US/UK export controls on advanced compute to China
regulatory.description: Neoverse V-series processors exceed US/UK export-control performance thresholds for China-bound HPC/AI/advanced-compute use, requiring export licenses that are difficult and unpredictable to obtain; further tightening could materially restrict PRC sales of Arm's highest-value data center IP.

regulatory.risk: US Treasury outbound investment rule (Exec. Order 14105)
regulatory.description: Final rule effective January 2025 restricts certain US-person investment in PRC semiconductor/AI companies; could affect Arm's PRC customers, suppliers, or Arm China over time.
Participation in standards bodies could require licensing patents on reasonable-and-non-discriminatory terms, limiting pricing power on certain IP.
UK National Security and Investment Act and CFIUS-style reviews could delay or block acquisitions (e.g., DreamBig) or impose conditions.

macro.description: Royalty revenue is a function of end-chip shipment volumes, which are tied to smartphone, PC, auto, and data-center capex cycles; industry downturns, inventory corrections, or a pause in AI capex spending would flow directly through to Arm's royalties and new license bookings.

PRC accounted for ~18% of FY2026 revenue; Taiwan-based foundries (effectively all of Arm's customers' advanced-node manufacturing) sit in a geopolitical flashpoint, and PRC-Taiwan tensions or broader US-China trade conflict could disrupt Arm's largest customers' supply chains and Arm's own PRC revenue access.

A large share of current growth narrative (data center royalty doubling, AGI CPU ramp) depends on hyperscalers sustaining very high AI infrastructure capex; any slowdown in AI buildout would disproportionately hit Arm's fastest-growing, most richly-valued growth driver.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Semiconductor industry structurally growing on AI/data-center, automotive electrification, and IoT demand, offset by a mature/slow-growth core smartphone market where Arm already holds near-monopoly share; management's own TAM slides describe AI-related addressable market expanding from roughly $400-500B (FY2026) toward $1.5T+ by FY2031, with data center CPU capacity needs cited as a >$100B opportunity by 2030.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high - royalty revenue tracks global chip shipment volumes (smartphones, PCs, servers, autos), which are cyclical and sensitive to consumer spending, enterprise IT capex, and (increasingly) hyperscaler AI capex budgets; license revenue is lumpier and tied to the timing of a limited number of large annual deals.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low direct balance-sheet sensitivity (asset-light model, minimal debt historically), but high indirect sensitivity via its growth-stock valuation multiple and via the capex appetite of AI infrastructure spenders, which is itself rate-sensitive.
key_input_costs: Engineering/R&D talent (84% of global headcount is engineering-focused)
Foundry capacity and wafer costs for the new Arm AGI CPU production-silicon business (TSMC advanced nodes)

recent_developments.event: Reported Q2 FY2027 (quarter ended Sept 30, 2026) results: revenue $1,443M (+27% YoY, best-ever Q2), License & Other revenue +50% YoY to $773M, Royalty revenue +8% YoY to $670M, non-GAAP diluted EPS $0.52 (+33% YoY) vs GAAP diluted EPS $0.12 (down from $0.22, pressured by $46.6M of fair-value losses on equity investments); annualized contract value $1,790M (+12%); non-GAAP operating margin 44.2%.
Issued Q3 FY2027 guidance: revenue $1.54B +/- $50M, non-GAAP diluted EPS $0.56 +/- $0.04, non-GAAP opex ~$825M; reiterated confidence in up to $2B cumulative Arm AGI CPU revenue across FY2027-28.
Data center/hyperscaler royalties doubled YoY; management said Arm-based share of silicon at top hyperscalers exceeded 50% in calendar 2025 and is tracking toward >60% by end of calendar 2026.

Arm AGI CPU purchase orders now extend through calendar 2027; Oracle Cloud Infrastructure disclosed plans to offer Arm AGI CPU instances starting 2027; first commercial deliveries remain on track for fiscal Q4 2027.

CEO Rene Haas appointed (part-time) Chief Executive Officer of SoftBank Group International, a role management says is intended to deepen integration between Arm and SoftBank's AI/semiconductor portfolio companies, but which the company itself flags as a potential conflict-of-interest and time-allocation risk.

Launched the Arm AGI CPU, Arm's first production silicon product for AI data centers, co-developed with Meta as lead partner; marks Arm's historic entry into selling its own chips rather than only licensing IP.

Q4/FY2026 results showed full-year revenue of $4,920M (+23% YoY): License & Other revenue $2,307M (+25%), Royalty revenue $2,613M (+21%); FY2026 non-GAAP operating income $2,115M, beating the internal bonus-plan target of $2,065M.

Completed sale of the Artisan foundation IP business (standard cell libraries, memory compilers, general-purpose I/Os) to Cadence Design Systems for a $131.0M pre-tax gain, narrowing Arm's portfolio to core CPU/GPU/NPU/system IP, CSS, and now production silicon.
Entered a definitive agreement to acquire DreamBig Semiconductor for ~$265M to add advanced networking/chiplet capability; expected to close by end of Q2 FY2027, subject to regulatory approval.

Jury in the Qualcomm/Nuvia litigation reached a split verdict; court later affirmed the verdict and granted Qualcomm judgment as a matter of law on the Nuvia breach claim. Arm has appealed to the Third Circuit; a separate Qualcomm suit against Arm Limited was consolidated into the ongoing case, with trial expected Q4 calendar 2026.

items.notes: Implies roughly 25%+ YoY growth continuing the FY2026/Q2 FY2027 trend; no explicit full-year FY2027 revenue range disclosed in the 6-K exhibit.
Follows a Q2 FY2027 beat of $0.52 non-GAAP EPS against a prior guided range of $0.43-$0.51.
Reflects continued R&D investment in Neoverse, CSS, and the Arm AGI CPU silicon ramp.

Management said confidence in hitting this target increased given purchase orders extending through calendar 2027 and OCI's planned 2027 AGI CPU cloud instances; first commercial deliveries targeted for fiscal Q4 2027.
Up from >50% in calendar 2025 and ~15% in calendar 2024, per management commentary on data-center royalty trajectory.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Rene Haas framed Q2 FY2027 as the company's best-ever second quarter and said Arm is 'becoming the compute platform of choice as AI transforms every market,' pointing to the 50% YoY licensing surge as a leading indicator for royalty growth as new designs tape out. Management emphasized data-center royalties doubling YoY and positioned the Arm AGI CPU silicon business as a second, structurally additive growth engine alongside the core IP-licensing model, while reiterating that no full-year FY2027 top-line guide was issued beyond the quarterly cadence.

bull_case: Royalty annuity plus accelerating license bookings: FY2026 License & Other revenue growth (+25%) and Q2 FY2027 (+50% YoY) are read by management and analysts as leading indicators of multi-year royalty growth as new Armv9/Neoverse/CSS designs tape out and ramp over the next 2-5 years

Genuine new growth vector in AI/data center: hyperscaler Arm-based silicon share has gone from ~15% (CY2024) to >50% (CY2025) and data-center royalties doubled YoY, while the Arm AGI CPU opens a second, higher-dollar-content production-silicon revenue stream (guided up to $2B cumulative FY2027-28, with a much larger multi-year ambition publicly discussed by the CEO)

Durable moat in the core franchise: >99% share of mobile applications processors, a 22-million-developer software ecosystem, and ~350 billion cumulative chips shipped make Arm very difficult to dislodge from its existing installed base in the near term, even as RISC-V gains share elsewhere

High incremental margins: as an IP/royalty business, each additional dollar of royalty revenue carries very high incremental margin (non-GAAP operating margin already ~44%), so continued top-line growth should disproportionately benefit profitability outside of the new, lower-margin silicon segment
Diversification beyond mobile: automotive, robotics (Physical AI), IoT, and networking are all growing contributors that reduce Arm's historical dependence on the now-mature smartphone cycle
bear_case: Elevated customer concentration and strategic conflict risk: ~57% of FY2026 revenue from the top five customers (including Arm China and SoftBank), and Arm's own entry into production silicon (Arm AGI CPU) directly competes with some of the same semiconductor/OEM customers it depends on for licensing revenue, risking retaliation, disintermediation, or accelerated RISC-V adoption

RISC-V and in-house silicon are real, growing alternatives: several of Arm's largest customers are simultaneously investors in RISC-V and/or designing their own cores (Qualcomm/Nuvia litigation is a direct example), and if the open-standard ecosystem matures faster than expected, Arm's long-run royalty-per-chip economics could compress, especially outside the mobile stronghold

SoftBank governance overhang: SoftBank's ~86.4% ownership, board influence, and the CEO's new part-time SoftBank Group International role create related-party and conflict-of-interest risk that minority ADS holders cannot fully diligence or control, and the Arm China relationship (~16-18% of revenue) remains outside Arm's operational control with a history of governance disputes and payment friction

Valuation and execution risk in the new silicon business: the Arm AGI CPU pivots Arm into a capital-intensive, inventory-bearing, foundry-dependent business for the first time, exposing it to yield, supply-chain, and margin risks the pure-IP model never had, at a moment when the stock already prices in a large, AI-capex-dependent growth narrative - any slowdown in hyperscaler AI spending would hit Arm's most richly valued growth driver hardest

Geopolitical and export-control exposure: PRC revenue (~18% of FY2026 total) depends on an independently operated Arm China JV and is increasingly gated by US/UK export controls on the highest-performance Neoverse processors destined for China, while Taiwan-concentrated foundry manufacturing leaves Arm's entire customer base exposed to cross-strait tension
